strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of video anomaly detection: the same event may be normal or abnormal depending on user requirements. Explicit language conditioning offers a useful interface for this problem.
PreVAD is a potentially valuable resource, with 35,279 videos, hierarchical categories, anomaly descriptions, and frame-level validation annotations across several domains.

Evaluation spans seven datasets and includes a useful same-training-data comparison. LaGoVAD consistently improves detection over PreVAD-trained VadCLIP, including 74.25 versus 67.43 AP on XD-Violence and 62.60 versus 50.59 AUC on DoTA.
Table 4 provides evidence that dynamic synthesis, negative mining, and language conditioning each improve average cross-dataset performance.
weaknesses: The central contribution—adaptation to changing anomaly definitions—is insufficiently evaluated. Quantitative experiments use fixed dataset-specific category prompts; only two qualitative examples change definitions for the same video. A systematic benchmark with paired definitions, relabeled temporal annotations, and language-conditioned baselines is needed to distinguish genuine definition following from ordinary cross-dataset generalization.

The claim that conditioning on the definition avoids concept drift is stronger than the argument supports. Section 3 assumes that video and definition fully determine the label; this does not establish that the learned conditional mapping generalizes to unseen definitions. Training alternates category names and descriptions, but does not clearly specify examples where the same behavior receives different binary labels under different definitions.

The dataset's independence and annotation quality are not adequately established in the supplied manuscript. Independently collecting web videos does not exclude overlap with web-sourced evaluation datasets. There is no reported cross-benchmark duplicate audit, source-disjoint splitting procedure, quantitative description-quality assessment, or annotator agreement. Licensing and privacy handling for collected surveillance footage are also unspecified.

The technical novelty beyond existing CLIP-based VAD is relatively incremental, and comparisons do not fully isolate it. The synthesis module lacks comparisons against simple random concatenation or duration-matched augmentation, while negative mining lacks a standard contrastive-loss control. A direct baseline that scores user-selected anomaly classes would be particularly relevant to the proposed paradigm.

The contrastive objective contains substantive specification errors. Given the stated feature shapes, Equation 15 requires a transpose. Equation 17 sums over the visual index while holding the text index fixed, rather than normalizing over text candidates as a video-to-text loss should. The implementation must be clarified before the stated bidirectional objective can be verified.

Reproducibility and interpretation remain limited: implementation settings, exact prompts, synthesis sampling details, and annotation procedures are deferred to supplementary material absent from the supplied PDF, and no variability estimates are reported. Classification superiority is also overstated: UCF-Crime F1 decreases from 17.81 for PreVAD-trained VadCLIP to 16.64 for LaGoVAD, despite higher accuracy; the F1 averaging convention and class-level results are needed.

(17) normalizes over visual rows rather than text columns, inconsistent with the claimed video-to-text loss. These may be notation errors, but the intended implementation needs clarification.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of conventional video anomaly detection: users may change which events count as abnormal. Conditioning detection on language is a useful direction with clear practical motivation.

PreVAD is a substantial potential resource: 35,279 videos spanning 209.5 hours, with hierarchical categories and anomaly descriptions. The appendix documents sources, annotation procedures, and many implementation details.

The seven-dataset transfer evaluation is broad. Compared with VadCLIP trained on the same PreVAD data, LaGoVAD improves detection on all seven datasets, including XD-Violence AP from 67.43 to 74.25 and DoTA AUC from 50.59 to 62.60.

Component ablations support the utility of video synthesis and negative mining. Protocol 2 also makes a useful attempt to evaluate changing anomaly definitions explicitly rather than relying entirely on cross-dataset transfer.
weaknesses: The central claim of avoiding concept drift is stronger than the formulation establishes. Section 3 assumes that the conditional relationship between labels, videos, and definitions is invariant; conditioning on the definition does not itself establish that assumption or guarantee generalization to unseen definitions. The implementation principally accepts sets of category names or descriptions, and training does not clearly demonstrate the same event receiving different labels under different definitions.

The dedicated concept-drift evaluation is too limited to establish general language-guided adaptability. It uses five category subsets on only two datasets, without systematic tests of contextual rules, negation, paraphrases, or compositional definitions. Crucially, the language-guidance ablation is reported for ordinary cross-dataset detection, not drift@5, so improvements under the central protocol are not isolated from stronger underlying recognition.

Protocol 2 relabels videos using their category membership, but the paper itself demonstrates videos containing multiple anomaly types in Figure I. It does not explain how frame-level ground truth is corrected when an excluded-category video contains an included event, or vice versa. This creates an unresolved validity concern for the principal concept-drift benchmark.

The most informative simple baseline is missing: aggregate the scores of a pretrained or PreVAD-trained open-vocabulary temporal classifier over the user-selected anomaly categories. Such a baseline would test whether conditional fusion adds value beyond category selection. The Qwen comparisons also convert predicted intervals into binary scores, producing much coarser ROC/PR operating points than the proposed continuous scores; these results require qualification.

The dataset's quality and independence are insufficiently verified. No quantitative audit of generated descriptions, annotation agreement, or residual label errors is reported. Independently collecting web videos does not establish disjointness from web-sourced evaluation datasets; a source-level and visual near-duplicate audit is needed to substantiate the zero-shot claims.

Dynamic synthesis knows the location of an abnormal source video, not the true anomaly boundaries within it. Nevertheless, its positive pseudo-label term encourages every frame in that source interval to receive a high anomaly score. The resulting label noise and possible reliance on concatenation boundaries are not adequately examined. The negative-mining loss likewise assumes low-scoring frames are valid background without measuring the reliability of that assumption.

Experimental uncertainty and several reporting details remain unresolved. There are no repeated-run or subset-level uncertainty estimates, despite small margins such as 0.856 versus 0.852 MSAD drift AUC. Exact evaluation prompts, the DoTA normalization procedure, and model-selection rules are insufficiently specified. The claim of superiority across classification results also overlooks UCF F1, where LaGoVAD scores 16.64 versus 17.81 for same-data VadCLIP.

The dataset ethics statement incorrectly treats public availability as sufficient to rule out privacy and ethical issues. Given identifiable surveillance subjects, violence footage, and third-party sources, the paper should document licensing compatibility, privacy safeguards, removal procedures, and annotator protections. Promising annotations and download scripts does not resolve these concerns.

strengths: The problem is practically meaningful: anomaly labels can change with user requirements, and conditioning detection on textual definitions is a useful direction.
PreVAD is a substantial potential resource, comprising 35,279 videos with hierarchical labels and anomaly descriptions. The collection pipeline and source statistics are described in useful detail.

The seven-dataset evaluation provides concrete evidence of transfer improvements. Against VadCLIP trained on the same PreVAD data, LaGoVAD improves detection on every dataset, including XD-Violence AP from 67.43 to 74.25 and DoTA AUC from 50.59 to 62.60.
Component ablations support the usefulness of synthesis and negative mining. Protocol 2 also goes beyond standard cross-dataset evaluation by explicitly changing which categories count as abnormal.
weaknesses: The central claim exceeds the demonstrated scope. Conditioning on an anomaly definition avoids the specified concept drift only if P(Y|V,Z) remains invariant and the definition captures the relevant labeling policy; Section 3 assumes this rather than establishing it. Protocol 2 tests five category subsets on two datasets, providing limited evidence for arbitrary natural-language policies, contextual rules, or negation.

The most informative baseline for the central contribution is missing: an open-vocabulary temporal classifier whose scores are aggregated over the user-selected abnormal categories. Such a baseline could handle the subset changes in Protocol 2 without the proposed fusion mechanism. Comparing against a definition-insensitive VadCLIP detection branch does not isolate this distinction.

The zero-shot dataset claims need stronger verification. PreVAD draws from web compilations and existing video datasets, but no cross-benchmark duplicate or near-duplicate audit is reported. Independent collection does not establish disjointness from web-sourced test benchmarks. The claimed description quality also lacks a quantitative human audit or agreement analysis.

Dynamic synthesis introduces unresolved label noise. The inserted abnormal video has only a video-level label, yet its entire interval receives positive pseudo-labels. Equation 10 therefore encourages high scores on normal frames within that video, while omitting a corresponding framewise negative term for inserted normal segments. The ablations show empirical utility but do not establish the claimed improvement in learning temporal boundaries.

The concept-drift comparisons need better controls and uncertainty reporting. Qwen outputs are converted to binary scores while other methods supply continuous scores, complicating AUC/AP comparisons. No per-definition results, repeated-run variation, or confidence intervals are provided; some margins are small, such as MSAD drift AUC of 0.856 versus 0.852.

Important reproducibility details remain incomplete, including the full inference prompts, precise DoTA normalization, and how training constructs differing definitions and corresponding labels. The blanket superiority claim also overlooks UCF classification F1: LaGoVAD scores 16.64 versus 17.81 for VadCLIP trained on PreVAD.

The dataset statement incorrectly treats public availability as sufficient to dismiss privacy and ethical issues. For identifiable surveillance and violence footage, the paper should document source permissions, privacy handling, and safeguards for annotators.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of conventional video anomaly detection: an event’s abnormality can change with user requirements. Conditioning detection on textual anomaly definitions is practically useful.

PreVAD is a substantial potential resource: 35,279 videos spanning 209.5 hours, with hierarchical categories, anomaly descriptions, and temporal validation annotations. The collection pipeline and source statistics are described in useful detail.

Cross-dataset evaluation is broad, covering seven datasets. Against VadCLIP trained on the same PreVAD data, LaGoVAD improves detection on all seven, including XD-Violence AP from 67.43 to 74.25 and DoTA AUC from 50.59 to 62.60. This provides concrete evidence beyond simply benefiting from additional training data.

Component ablations support the proposed regularizers: removing both reduces average detection performance from 76.42 to 71.31. The supplementary architecture and optimization details help reproducibility.
The changing-definition evaluation is a useful initial benchmark, and the qualitative example demonstrates that predictions can respond to a changed definition.
weaknesses: The central claim of flexible language-defined abnormality is evaluated mainly through subsets of existing category labels. This does not establish compliance with contextual rules, negation, compositional definitions, or policy changes such as the motivating mask example. Training also lacks a clearly described mechanism for presenting the same event as normal and abnormal under different definitions. The evidence supports category-conditioned detection more strongly than general user-defined anomaly detection.

Protocol 2 needs stronger controls. A baseline that aggregates an open-vocabulary classifier’s scores over the requested categories would help distinguish language-conditioned detection from category selection. The language-guidance ablation is reported under Protocol 1, rather than the changing-definition protocol that directly tests its purpose. Relabeling videos by their assigned category is also potentially problematic when multiple anomaly types co-occur, as the paper itself illustrates.

The zero-shot claim lacks a documented overlap audit. PreVAD uses web videos, accident compilations, and RWF-2000, while several evaluation datasets also contain web-sourced footage. Independent collection does not establish disjoint content; source-level and perceptual deduplication against the test sets are needed. Description quality is likewise asserted without a quantitative human audit or reported agreement statistics.

The formulation does not establish that conditioning on Z avoids concept drift. It assumes that P(Y|V,Z) remains invariant and that the supplied definition captures all relevant context. Equation 2 is a probability decomposition, not a guarantee of generalization. The methodological novelty is otherwise primarily a combination of familiar cross-attention, MIL, concatenation augmentation, and contrastive learning.

Dynamic synthesis introduces uncertain frame supervision: the full abnormal anchor video receives positive pseudo-labels despite potentially containing normal frames, and the final loss term encourages positive scores throughout that interval. The paper does not measure this label noise or isolate the contribution of this term from concatenation and MIL.

Several evaluation details weaken confidence in the reported margins. There are no repeated-run uncertainties or per-definition results; Qwen models are evaluated using binary boundary-derived scores against continuous-score detectors; and DoTA score normalization is underspecified. The claim of superiority across all classification results is also too broad: UCF F1 is 16.64, below the same-data VadCLIP result of 17.81.

Dataset governance is insufficiently addressed. Appendix C.1 treats public availability as establishing the absence of privacy and ethical issues, despite collecting surveillance footage and violent incidents. Source licensing, privacy safeguards, removal procedures, and annotator welfare require a substantive account. The promised resource release is not accompanied by an accessible artifact in the submission.
